title: Coherent contracted powers of a torsor
statement: Let X be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], G an abelian sheaf on the small Zariski site X_{\mathrm{Zar}} [def-sc-zariski-site], and T a G-torsor [def-sc-gm-torsor]. Define the inverse torsor T^{-1} to be the sheaf T with action g\cdot' t:=(-g)\cdot t. For n>0 let T^{\otimes n} be the n-fold contracted product T\wedge\cdots\wedge T, for n<0 let T^{\otimes n}=(T^{-1})^{\wedge |n|}, and let T^{\otimes0}=G, where \wedge is the antidiagonal contracted product [lem-sc-torsor-h1]. (a) Each T^{\otimes n} is a G-torsor. (b) For all m,n\in\mathbf Z there are canonical G-torsor isomorphisms \mu_{m,n}:T^{\otimes m}\wedge T^{\otimes n}\xrightarrow{\sim}T^{\otimes(m+n)}. These include T\wedge T^{-1}\cong G, sending [t,s] to the unique local section h of G with h\cdot s=t; the degree-zero isomorphisms are the unit constraints. The \mu_{m,n} are unital, associative, and commutative: \mu_{n,m}\circ\mathrm{swap}=\mu_{m,n}, where swap interchanges the two contracted-product factors and commutativity uses that G is abelian. Moreover T^{\otimes1}=T and the degree-zero unit constraint G\wedge T\cong T is the original G-action.

proof.text: Take a Zariski cover with a section t_0 of T. Write a\in G for the section a\cdot t_0 of T, and b\in G for the section b\cdot' t_0=(-b)\cdot t_0 of T^{-1}. Negation makes the latter action free and transitive. On this cover the antidiagonal relation (g\cdot x,(-g)\cdot y) identifies a pair of coordinates (a,b) with (a+g,b-g); hence addition (a,b)\mapsto a+b identifies the contracted product with the translation torsor G. Iterating this quotient gives a coordinate equal to the sum of the coordinates of every factor, for either sign, so every nonzero power is locally the translation torsor. Degree zero is G itself. These local torsor structures are those of the sheaf contracted products and thus restrict and glue.

source.place: Worker's argument: local trivializations and the contracted-product group law

proof.text: In the coordinates of step 1, define \mu_{m,n} by addition G\wedge G\to G, [a,b]\mapsto a+b. This is a G-equivariant isomorphism: the antidiagonal relation preserves the sum and every class has the unique representative [a+b,0]. To check independence of t_0, write another local section as t_1=c\cdot t_0. The coordinate of a T-factor changes from a to a-c, while that of a T^{-1}-factor changes from b to b+c. Thus the coordinate of degree k changes by -kc (also for k=0), and the source sum changes by -(m+n)c, exactly as the target coordinate does. The local maps therefore agree on overlaps and glue to canonical sheaf isomorphisms. For degree zero, [g,a]\mapsto g+a is precisely the original action; one factor gives T^{\otimes1}=T.

source.place: Worker's argument: concatenation, cancellation, and degree-zero unit constraints

proof.text: On any trivializing open, both associative composites send [a,b,d] to a+b+d. The swapped composite sends [a,b] to b+a=a+b because G is abelian. The degree-zero maps send [0,a] and [a,0] to a, so both unit laws hold. Equality of sheaf morphisms can be checked on the trivializing cover; hence these identities hold globally for all signed degrees, including m=0 or n=0.

source.place: Worker's argument: associativity, commutativity, and units of contracted product

proof.text: For t=a\cdot t_0 and s=b\cdot' t_0=(-b)\cdot t_0, the unique h with h\cdot s=t is h=a+b, which is exactly \mu_{1,-1} from step 2. Replacing the pair by (g\cdot t,(-g)\cdot' s) changes the two coordinates to a+g and b-g, so h is unchanged. Conversely h is represented locally by [h\cdot s,s]; if s is replaced by d\cdot' s, this pair changes by the antidiagonal relation with -d, so its class is independent of s. For degree n and -n the same coordinate formula sums all positive and inverse coordinates; it is \mu_{n,-n}, whose inverse exists by step 2.
